status: playable content pack for integration into the existing app

session_design.feedback: Show +Knowledge briefly, then disappear. Do not add extra currencies.
session_design.mastery_logic: Points reward play; mastery tracks what the player actually knows. Missed items return sooner. Recall-before-reveal and share cards use self-rating.
pacing_rules: Never show more than two standard multiple-choice encounters in a row.
New concepts should usually appear first as a short DISCOVER card, then be tested later.
Keep ordinary prompt text under ~28 words when possible.
Keep ordinary reveals to 1–2 short sentences.
Use three answer choices when a fourth choice adds no useful discrimination.
Do not use a debate as the first exposure to either thinker.
End every session with KEEP THIS, not another quiz.
session_design.new_player_onboarding: Use three curated starter sessions before fully adaptive play. Teach the interface without explaining the scheduling system.

modes.SAME QUESTION: compare historically grounded answers without choosing a political winner
modes.THEN → NOW: apply an old lens to a generic present-day scenario
modes.WHY THEN: connect idea to the historical circumstances that made it significant
modes.DISCOVER: brief first exposure to a strong idea; tap to continue
modes.MATCH: drag or tap to match thinkers with ideas; no typing

hidden_lens_rules: Repeatedly surface questions of power, ownership, institutions, collective capacity, structure, and what happens after protest.
Use WHO IS “WE”? as a recurring question, not a scored doctrine or formal thread.
Distinguish access from control and individual mobility from structural change.
The hidden Black-radical lens shapes which questions recur; it does not predetermine the player’s political answers.
Debates present competing strategies sympathetically and never score a political winner.
content_rules: A new idea should usually appear as DISCOVER before it is tested.
Never show more than two standard multiple-choice screens in a row.
Ordinary prompts should stay short enough to read comfortably on a phone.
Use BEST FIT for strategic or interpretive comparisons.
RECALL and SHARE use self-rating rather than AI grading.
Misses return sooner; never remove Knowledge.
WORDS remains reserved for verified literal quotations and is not expanded by this pack.
TODAY claims require fresh sourcing; generic transfer scenarios are allowed when they do not assert current facts.

discovery_cards.title: START HERE
discovery_cards.statement: Black history doesn’t start in 1619. It starts in Africa.
discovery_cards.reveal: Enslavement is a rupture in a longer African history—not the beginning of Black existence.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — Africa

discovery_cards.title: DU BOIS
discovery_cards.statement: You can know yourself—and still feel yourself being measured through somebody else’s eyes.
discovery_cards.reveal: Du Bois called this tension double consciousness.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Introduction / The Souls of Black Folk

discovery_cards.title: ELLA BAKER
discovery_cards.statement: Strong leadership should leave more people capable of leading.
discovery_cards.reveal: Baker favored participatory leadership over a movement dependent on one public figure.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History + Four Hundred Souls — Ella Baker

discovery_cards.title: FREEDOM’S JOURNAL
discovery_cards.statement: Owning the platform can be part of owning the story.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black-controlled media gave Black communities a way to define themselves publicly.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — Freedom’s Journal

discovery_cards.title: RECONSTRUCTION
discovery_cards.statement: Ending slavery answered one question. Freedom created several more.
discovery_cards.reveal: Citizenship, voting, education, land, labor, and political power still had to be fought over.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls + Black AF History — Reconstruction

discovery_cards.title: IDA B. WELLS
discovery_cards.statement: Before accepting the story used to justify violence, check the evidence.
discovery_cards.reveal: Wells used reporting and statistics to challenge the myths used to defend lynching.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Ida B. Wells

discovery_cards.title: ZORA NEALE HURSTON
discovery_cards.statement: Black life did not need to become a protest message before it could become art.
discovery_cards.reveal: Hurston treated vernacular, folklore, humor, and ordinary life as worthy subjects themselves.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — Zora Neale Hurston

discovery_cards.title: MALCOLM X
discovery_cards.statement: A struggle for citizenship can also be framed as a struggle for human rights.
discovery_cards.reveal: Malcolm increasingly placed Black freedom inside a global story of self-determination and anticolonial struggle.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History + Four Hundred Souls — Malcolm X

discovery_cards.title: LAW HELPED CONSTRUCT RACE
discovery_cards.statement: Racist law didn’t just enforce race. It helped define what race meant.
discovery_cards.reveal: Colonial law did not merely reflect racial categories; it helped harden them by assigning unequal status, rights, and inheritance.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls + Black AF History — 1664–1709 chapters; Black AF History 'How White People Were Invented'

discovery_cards.title: BACON’S REBELLION AND DIVIDED INTERESTS
discovery_cards.statement: Race and class can divide people who share material problems.
discovery_cards.reveal: Colonial elites had incentives to sharpen racial divisions among laboring people who could otherwise share economic grievances.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1674–1679: Bacon’s Rebellion

discovery_cards.title: MARRONAGE AND AUTONOMOUS COMMUNITIES
discovery_cards.statement: Sometimes freedom meant escaping the system and building somewhere else.
discovery_cards.reveal: Some enslaved people pursued freedom by leaving slave society and building alternative communities such as maroon settlements and Fort Mose.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1719–1724: Maroons and Marronage; 1734–1739: From Fort Mose to Soul City

discovery_cards.title: THE SPIRITUALS
discovery_cards.statement: A song can carry history, faith, and strategy at the same time.
discovery_cards.reveal: Spirituals could carry theology, memory, coded meaning, endurance, and visions of freedom simultaneously.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1724–1729: The Spirituals

discovery_cards.title: FREEDOM CHURCH
discovery_cards.statement: The Black church became both a sanctuary and an organizing institution.
discovery_cards.reveal: Independent Black religious life became a place where faith, collective organization, mutual aid, and claims for freedom could meet.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — David George / freedom church; Savannah and early Black churches

discovery_cards.title: PHILLIS WHEATLEY
discovery_cards.statement: Wheatley had to write poems—and prove Black people could think.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black literary achievement challenged claims of Black intellectual inferiority while exposing the burden of having to prove humanity to a hostile public.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1764–1769: Phillis Wheatley

discovery_cards.title: LIBERTY’S CONTRADICTION
discovery_cards.statement: America preached universal liberty while deciding who counted as universal.
discovery_cards.reveal: Enlightenment and Revolutionary language about universal liberty coexisted with racial hierarchy and slavery, giving Black people both a contradiction to expose and a language to claim.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1749–1754: Race and the Enlightenment; 1774–1779: The American Revolution

discovery_cards.title: DENMARK VESEY
discovery_cards.statement: Rebellion required organization long before it required action.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black resistance could require secret networks, trust, planning, and a willingness to pursue collective freedom under severe repression.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1819–1824: Denmark Vesey

discovery_cards.title: MARIA STEWART
discovery_cards.statement: Stewart argued that Black freedom could not leave Black women behind.
discovery_cards.reveal: Stewart connected Black advancement to education, public voice, economic ambition, and the political agency of Black women.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1829–1834: Maria Stewart

discovery_cards.title: NATIONAL NEGRO CONVENTIONS
discovery_cards.statement: Movements need places to argue about strategy, not only places to protest.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black political thought developed through institutions where people debated abolition, education, migration, and strategy together.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1834–1839: The National Negro Conventions

discovery_cards.title: JAMES MCCUNE SMITH
discovery_cards.statement: McCune Smith fought racist 'science' with evidence and expertise.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black intellectuals used scholarship and professional expertise to challenge racial pseudoscience and supposedly objective claims of inferiority.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1844–1849: James McCune Smith, M.D.

discovery_cards.title: FREDERICK DOUGLASS
discovery_cards.statement: Douglass escaped slavery, then spent his life attacking the system itself.
discovery_cards.reveal: Douglass linked literacy, abolition, citizenship, political action, and the destruction of slavery; personal escape was not enough while the system remained.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1859–1864: Frederick Douglass

discovery_cards.title: ATLANTA WASHERWOMEN
discovery_cards.statement: Black washerwomen turned private labor into collective bargaining power.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black washerwomen used labor autonomy, common rates, mutual-aid traditions, and collective organization to increase control over their work.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — Atlanta / washerwomen and post-Reconstruction Black neighborhoods

discovery_cards.title: PLESSY AND THE CITIZENS’ COMMITTEE
discovery_cards.statement: Plessy was a defeat in court—and the product of organized resistance.
discovery_cards.reveal: Plessy v. Ferguson legalized 'separate but equal,' but the case itself grew from organized Black resistance to segregation.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1894–1899: Plessy v. Ferguson

discovery_cards.title: BOOKER T. WASHINGTON
discovery_cards.statement: Washington’s bet: build skills and wealth while navigating a hostile system.
discovery_cards.reveal: Washington emphasized industrial education, economic strength, and pragmatic advancement as a route toward Black progress in a hostile political environment.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls + Black AF History — 1899–1904: Booker T. Washington; Wells section

discovery_cards.title: W.E.B. DU BOIS — BLACK RECONSTRUCTION
discovery_cards.statement: Du Bois made enslaved people actors in emancipation, not spectators to it.
discovery_cards.reveal: Du Bois reframed Reconstruction and emancipation around Black agency, arguing that enslaved people helped destroy slavery by withdrawing labor and joining the freedom struggle.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Black Reconstruction / 'The General Strike' discussion

discovery_cards.title: IDA B. WELLS — LEVERAGE AND SELF-PROTECTION
discovery_cards.statement: Wells paired truth-telling with economic pressure and self-protection.
discovery_cards.reveal: Wells treated migration, boycotts, public exposure, and self-defense as forms of leverage when authorities would not protect Black communities.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Ida B. Wells section; Mob Rule discussion

discovery_cards.title: MARY CHURCH TERRELL
discovery_cards.statement: Terrell turned education and status into tools for public action.
discovery_cards.reveal: Terrell used education, writing, club work, anti-lynching advocacy, women’s rights, and direct challenges to segregation as mutually reinforcing forms of public action.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Mary Church Terrell section

discovery_cards.title: CALLIE HOUSE
discovery_cards.statement: The reparations movement had mass organizers more than a century ago.
discovery_cards.reveal: House helped build a mass reparations movement among formerly enslaved people through local chapters, churches, agents, and membership organization.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Ex-slave pension / Callie House discussion

discovery_cards.title: THE GREAT MIGRATION
discovery_cards.statement: Millions moved because geography itself could shape freedom.
discovery_cards.reveal: Migration became a strategy for pursuing safety, wages, political possibility, and autonomy, not simply a change of address.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1914–1919: The Great Migration

discovery_cards.title: HARLEM RENAISSANCE
discovery_cards.statement: The Harlem Renaissance was also a debate about who Black art was for.
discovery_cards.reveal: The Harlem Renaissance became an argument about who could define Black life and what Black art owed to politics, audiences, and white patronage.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1924–1929: The Harlem Renaissance

discovery_cards.title: JAMES BALDWIN
discovery_cards.statement: Baldwin refused narrow stories about what Black life was allowed to be.
discovery_cards.reveal: Baldwin pushed against narrow depictions of Black life and used autobiography, criticism, and global perspective to insist on fuller Black humanity.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1954–1959 cultural chapter / Notes of a Native Son discussion

discovery_cards.title: THE BLACK LEFT
discovery_cards.statement: The Black Left tied race to who owned, worked, and profited.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black radicals linked racial hierarchy to labor, capitalism, imperialism, and class instead of treating racism only as prejudice.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1944–1949: The Black Left

discovery_cards.title: MARY MCLEOD BETHUNE
discovery_cards.statement: Bethune built institutions outside government and leverage inside it.
discovery_cards.reveal: Bethune combined Black institution-building with access to federal decision-makers to pursue jobs, education, and policy opportunities.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Mary McLeod Bethune section

discovery_cards.title: A. PHILIP RANDOLPH
discovery_cards.statement: Randolph’s leverage came from people organized behind the threat.
discovery_cards.reveal: Randolph used the credible threat of mass protest to increase pressure on federal officials over employment discrimination.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Bethune / Randolph / Executive Order 8802 discussion

discovery_cards.title: BROWN V. BOARD
discovery_cards.statement: Brown changed the rule before it changed the reality.
discovery_cards.reveal: Brown overturned the constitutional basis for school segregation, while demonstrating that changing the legal rule and changing institutions are separate tasks.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1949–1954: The Road to Brown v. Board

discovery_cards.title: MONTGOMERY 1955 — ORGANIZER, ACTION, SYMBOL
discovery_cards.statement: Parks became the symbol because organizers were already prepared to move.
discovery_cards.reveal: Claudette Colvin, Rosa Parks, Jo Ann Robinson, the Women’s Political Council, lawyers, and local networks show that the person who acts, the person who organizes, and the person who becomes the symbol may be different people.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Women who desegregated Montgomery buses

discovery_cards.title: MARTIN LUTHER KING JR. — NONVIOLENT RESISTANCE
discovery_cards.statement: King’s nonviolence was a method of resistance, not passive acceptance.
discovery_cards.reveal: King treated disciplined nonviolent resistance as an organizing strategy for confronting injustice publicly, mobilizing broad participation, and applying moral and political pressure.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History + Four Hundred Souls — Civil Rights Movement / Black Power discussions

discovery_cards.title: STOKELY CARMICHAEL / KWAME TURE
discovery_cards.statement: Carmichael shifted the question from inclusion to political control.
discovery_cards.reveal: Carmichael/Ture emphasized Black political self-determination and evolved from civil-rights organizing toward Black Power and Pan-Africanism.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History + Four Hundred Souls — Black Power chapters

discovery_cards.title: FRED HAMPTON
discovery_cards.statement: Hampton built coalition around concrete needs, not vague solidarity.
discovery_cards.reveal: Hampton linked political education, community programs, and coalition across racial and ethnic groups around shared material interests.
discovery_cards.source: Black AF History — Fred Hampton / COINTELPRO section

discovery_cards.title: COMBAHEE RIVER COLLECTIVE
discovery_cards.statement: Combahee asked politics to see Black women whole, not one category at a time.
discovery_cards.reveal: Combahee argued that race, gender, class, and sexuality could operate simultaneously; Black women could build politics from their own position while still forming coalitions.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1974–1979: Combahee River Collective

discovery_cards.title: HIP-HOP GENERATION
discovery_cards.statement: Hip-hop became a political language without needing to look like a political meeting.
discovery_cards.reveal: Hip-hop became a space where a new generation narrated Black urban life, politics, creativity, alienation, and identity outside older movement forms.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1984–1989: The Hip-Hop Generation

discovery_cards.title: ANITA HILL AND BLACK WOMEN’S PUBLIC VOICE
discovery_cards.statement: Anita Hill exposed what happens when race and gender demand different loyalties.
discovery_cards.reveal: The Anita Hill hearings forced public debate over race, gender, sexual harassment, credibility, and whether Black women’s experiences could be subordinated to other political loyalties.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1989–1994: Anita Hill

discovery_cards.title: BLACK IMMIGRANT IDENTITY
discovery_cards.statement: Black identity can unite people without erasing where they came from.
discovery_cards.reveal: Blackness in the United States includes immigrants whose national, ethnic, and racial identities interact with a U.S. racial system that may read them simply as Black.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 1999–2004: The Black Immigrant

discovery_cards.title: VOTING RIGHTS AFTER SHELBY
discovery_cards.statement: Voting rights can expand, contract, and require protection again.
discovery_cards.reveal: The history of voting rights shows that legal protections can be weakened or reinterpreted after major victories, making political rights an ongoing institutional question.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 2009–2014: The Shelby Ruling

discovery_cards.title: BLACK LIVES MATTER — ORGANIZATIONAL FORM
discovery_cards.statement: Modern movements inherited old questions about leadership, power, and whose lives count.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black Lives Matter drew on Black feminist and grassroots traditions while using decentralized networks to organize in a media environment very different from mid-century movements.
discovery_cards.source: Four Hundred Souls — 2014–2019: Black Lives Matter

discovery_cards.title: RESPECTABILITY
discovery_cards.statement: Before people care, they ask whether you were proper, safe, moral.
discovery_cards.reveal: Respectability is the pressure or strategy of meeting dominant standards of behavior, appearance, morality, class, gender, sexuality, or public presentation in hopes of being treated as worthy of protection, opportunity, legitimacy, or sympathy.
discovery_cards.source: Black Perspectives audit synthesis + existing BLACK FOLK historical nodes — Vengeance feminism / fury and disrepute cluster; Montgomery; Wells; Terrell; Washington

discovery_cards.title: ABOLITION
discovery_cards.statement: Abolition asks what must end—and what must be built in its place.
discovery_cards.reveal: Abolition is a Black intellectual and political tradition that asks whether some systems must be ended rather than repaired—and what social institutions must exist so that the ending produces a durable form of freedom.
discovery_cards.source: Keywords for African American Studies — Abolition — Sarah Haley

discovery_cards.title: BLACK NATIONALISM
discovery_cards.statement: Black nationalism asks what Black self-determination requires in power, institutions, culture, and resources.
discovery_cards.reveal: Black nationalism is a varied tradition of Black self-determination. Different nationalists have emphasized territory, political unity, economic control, culture, independent institutions, or combinations of these.
discovery_cards.source: Keywords for African American Studies — Nationalism — Yohuru Williams

discovery_cards.title: PAN-AFRICANISM
discovery_cards.statement: Pan-Africanism tries to turn global Black connection into organized solidarity.
discovery_cards.reveal: Pan-Africanism is a family of political and cultural projects that tries to turn connections among African-descended peoples into deliberate solidarity, organization, or cooperation across national borders.
discovery_cards.source: Keywords for African American Studies — Pan-Africanism — Tsitsi Jaji

discovery_cards.title: CRIMINALIZATION
discovery_cards.statement: Criminalization asks who gets defined as dangerous—and who gains power from that label.
discovery_cards.reveal: Criminalization is the process through which laws, institutions, media, and social narratives define particular people, behaviors, or communities as dangerous and therefore more legitimately punishable or controllable.
discovery_cards.source: Keywords for African American Studies — Criminal — Dylan Rodríguez

discovery_cards.title: PREDATORY INCLUSION
discovery_cards.statement: Predatory inclusion is access granted on unequal or exploitative terms.
discovery_cards.reveal: Predatory inclusion describes access granted to people previously excluded from a market or institution, but on unequal or exploitative terms that can reproduce extraction rather than equal power.
discovery_cards.source: Black Perspectives audit synthesis — Paige Glotzer on Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor's Race for Profit — predatory inclusion

starter_sessions.title: WHO DEFINES THE STORY?
starter_sessions.keep_this: History changes when you change who gets to define the story.
starter_sessions.purpose: Introduce DISCOVER, multiple choice, and RECALL without exceeding two quiz screens in a row.

starter_sessions.title: WHAT DOES FREEDOM REQUIRE?
starter_sessions.keep_this: Ending a barrier and building freedom are not the same job.
starter_sessions.purpose: Introduce context, strategy comparison, recall, and timeline.

starter_sessions.title: HOW DOES POWER MOVE?
starter_sessions.keep_this: Attention matters. Organization, leverage, and leadership determine what happens next.
starter_sessions.purpose: Introduce evidence, organizing, fair comparison, connection, and SHARE.

v1_5_bridge_sessions.title: WHO GETS CALLED DANGEROUS?
v1_5_bridge_sessions.keep_this: Before punishment or protection, ask who was defined as dangerous—or worthy.
v1_5_bridge_sessions.purpose: Introduce Criminalization and Respectability together: who gets marked dangerous, who gets marked worthy, and who is pushed outside the story.

v1_5_bridge_sessions.title: ACCESS OR CONTROL?
v1_5_bridge_sessions.keep_this: Getting in and having control are different questions.
v1_5_bridge_sessions.purpose: Introduce Predatory Inclusion and Black Nationalism through access, terms, ownership, and decision-making.

v1_5_bridge_sessions.title: BLACKNESS ACROSS BORDERS
v1_5_bridge_sessions.keep_this: Connection across borders is real without becoming sameness across borders.
v1_5_bridge_sessions.purpose: Introduce Black immigrant identity, Diaspora as a concept, and Pan-Africanism as an organizing project.

v1_5_bridge_sessions.title: WHO IS “WE”?
v1_5_bridge_sessions.keep_this: When politics says “we,” ask whose life is being treated as the norm.
v1_5_bridge_sessions.purpose: Turn WHO IS “WE”? into a recurring reflex through Stewart, Combahee, and collective politics.

v1_5_bridge_sessions.title: WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE END?
v1_5_bridge_sessions.keep_this: Ending a system and building freedom are different jobs.
v1_5_bridge_sessions.purpose: Introduce Abolition inside LEAVE · REFORM · BUILD without making it the app’s predetermined political answer.

session_end.rule: KEEP THIS is one short idea from the session, never a paragraph.
